journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research

abstracts.abstract: This study proposes a novel theoretical framework integrating predictive coding principles with embodied cognition theory to explain speech perception mechanisms in adverse listening conditions. Traditional models of speech perception have predominantly focused on bottom-up acoustic analysis or top-down linguistic processing in isolation, failing to account for the dynamic interaction between listener expectations and sensory input. The proposed Predictive-Embodied Speech Perception (PESP) framework posits that speech perception emerges from continuous prediction-error minimization, where listeners actively generate forward models of expected auditory signals grounded in sensorimotor experience. We conducted a comprehensive theoretical analysis examining how this framework accounts for established phenomena in speech science, including the cocktail party effect, categorical perception, and perceptual learning under degraded listening conditions. Mathematical formulations were developed to characterize the interaction between prior expectations, sensory precision weighting, and motor simulation processes. The framework generates testable predictions regarding neural correlates of speech perception that differ substantially from predictions derived from conventional dual-stream models. This paradigm-shifting approach provides a unified theoretical account that bridges speech perception with broader cognitive neuroscience principles, offering new directions for understanding communication disorders and developing targeted intervention strategies. The PESP framework represents a fundamental reconceptualization of how the auditory system processes and comprehends speech across diverse acoustic environments.

This study advances current understanding of language processing deficits in individuals with specific language impairment (SLI) by extending the Procedural Circuit Deficit Hypothesis through the incorporation of Bayesian computational principles. Previous theoretical accounts have attributed language deficits in SLI to selective impairments in procedural memory systems, yet these models have struggled to explain the heterogeneity of linguistic profiles observed across affected populations. We present a refined theoretical model that conceptualizes language acquisition and processing as probabilistic inference processes supported by complementary declarative and procedural memory systems. The Bayesian Procedural Framework proposes that SLI emerges from suboptimal integration of prior linguistic knowledge with noisy procedural computations, rather than from categorical procedural system damage. Through systematic analysis of computational simulations and re-examination of existing behavioral and neuroimaging data, we demonstrate that this framework provides superior explanatory power for phenomena including irregular verb inflection, complex syntax processing, and rapid automatized naming deficits characteristic of SLI. The model generates precise predictions regarding individual differences in language outcomes based on variations in prior knowledge quality and procedural noise parameters. These theoretical advances have direct implications for understanding the underlying mechanisms of language disorders and inform the development of more personalized intervention approaches targeting the specific computational deficits identified within this refined framework.

This paper presents an innovative multimodal assessment system for early identification of speech and language disorders in pediatric populations, addressing critical gaps in current screening methodologies that rely primarily on parent report measures. The Automated Speech-Language Evaluation System (ASLES) integrates automated speech recognition, acoustic analysis of voice parameters, and natural language processing of spontaneous speech samples to generate comprehensive diagnostic profiles. The system collects data through child-friendly tablet-based tasks that elicit specific linguistic structures while simultaneously capturing suprasegmental and segmental speech features. Advanced machine learning algorithms analyze phonological inventories, morphosyntactic complexity, and pragmatic communication indicators to identify patterns associated with various communication disorders. A groundbreaking feature of ASLES is its real-time phonetic analysis module that provides articulatory precision feedback, enabling differentiation between phonetic and phonemic errors with clinical accuracy. Validation studies with 847 children aged 3-6 years demonstrated sensitivity of 0.89 and specificity of 0.92 for identifying language disorders, significantly outperforming traditional screening approaches. The system generates detailed clinical reports mapping assessment findings to diagnostic categories while maintaining explainability essential for clinical decision-making. ASLES represents a paradigm shift in speech-language assessment by providing objective, automated, and ecologically valid evaluation tools that can be deployed in diverse healthcare settings to improve early detection of communication disorders.

This study describes the development and clinical validation of an enhanced digital hearing aid fitting system incorporating real-time speech intelligibility prediction and adaptive signal processing optimization. Existing fitting software relies on prescriptive methods derived from population-based audiometric thresholds, often failing to account for individual variability in speech perception abilities and specific listening demands. The proposed Adaptive Fitting Optimization System (AFOS) integrates patient-specific speech-in-noise assessment results with machine learning models trained on extensive audiometric databases to generate individualized amplification prescriptions. The system incorporates a novel speech intelligibility index calculator that adapts processing parameters based on real-time acoustic environment classification and predicted signal-to-noise ratio benefits. Clinical validation was conducted with 124 adults with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss across three hearing clinic sites. Results demonstrated that AFOS-fitted participants achieved statistically significant improvements in speech recognition thresholds (mean improvement of 3.2 dB SNR) and self-reported listening effort reduction compared to conventional fitting methods. The system includes an intuitive clinician interface with automated verification protocols ensuring proper device function and patient satisfaction. The adaptive nature of AFOS represents substantial methodological advancement over static fitting approaches, enabling precision audiology that tailors amplification characteristics to individual auditory processing profiles and real-world communication needs.
